chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Wallad al-Hannat, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a contracted slave (mukatab) whose master stipulated a condition upon him when he contracted him: that he would pay compensation to a man if he committed a crime against him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he has paid something from his contract, he is fined for his crime in proportion to what he has paid from his contract, to the free man. If he is unable to pay anything from the right of the crime, that is taken from the wealth of the master who contracted him.'

I said: 'And if the crime was against a slave?' He said: 'A similar amount is paid to the master of the slave whom the contracted slave injured, and there is no retaliation (taqass) between the contracted slave and the slave if the contracted slave has paid something from his contract. If he has not paid anything from his contract, then the slave is retaliated from him, or the master is fined for every crime the contracted slave committed, because he is his slave, as long as he has not paid anything from his contract.'
ai.seo_question: What is the financial liability of a contracted slave (mukatab) who injures a free person or a slave?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the nuanced jurisprudence of *jinayah* (blood money/damages) for a *mukatab* (freed slave under contract), distinguishing liability based on the proportion of the contract paid. It highlights the transitional legal status of the *mukatab*, where partial payment grants limited autonomy in bearing financial penalties, while full master liability persists until the contract is complete. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on equity in manumission, ensuring that the slave's evolving freedom correlates with their legal responsibility.
